document.title: Your Meeting on Usama bin Laden (Talking Points)
document.authors: Assistant Secretary Karl F. Inderfurth to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Department of State
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
document.note: [Secret/NODIS] Talking points noting that negotiations with the Taliban and Pakistan on bin Laden have failed and his network still threatens American lives. The December meeting with Nawaz Sharif is an opportunity to press the message. The Taliban brush-off of the indictment may signal a move from tolerance to more active support. Excised.

events.description: Planned meeting of Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif with the US President, to be used to press Pakistan on Taliban and Bin Laden.
Memo of talking points for Albright on Bin Laden, the Taliban and diplomatic pressure.
Planned meeting between Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and the US President, seen as a chance to press the Taliban/bin Laden issue.
Assistant Secretary Inderfurth gives Secretary Albright talking points for her meeting on Usama bin Laden.
The US tells the Taliban it holds them and their supporters responsible for bin Laden's actions because they provide sanctuary to him and his network.
The US applies diplomatic pressure on the Taliban to expel bin Laden to a country where he would face justice. The efforts have not yet succeeded.
The Taliban brushed off the US indictment of bin Laden and other evidence, which may signal a shift from tolerating his presence to more active support.

relationships.detail: The Taliban gave their word to prevent terrorism from Afghan soil and then broke the promise.
relationships.quote: They gave us their word they would do so but have broken this promise.

relationships.detail: The US has tried to enlist a redacted party to keep pressuring the Taliban. It is plausibly Pakistan, which asked what incentives the US could offer the Taliban, but the redaction makes this uncertain.
relationships.quote: has queried us directly regarding incentives that we could provide the Taliban.

sources_cited: US indictment of Bin Laden (referred to as 'our indictment')
key_claims: The US held the Taliban and its supporters responsible for Bin Laden's actions because they provide sanctuary.
The Taliban broke their promise to prevent terrorism being staged from Afghan soil.
Divisions exist within the Taliban over sheltering Bin Laden, but his ties to Mullah Omar protect him, and the US thought these fissures should be exploited.
The US sought third-country pressure, with Sharif's meeting as a chance to press Pakistan, and diplomatic efforts to expel Bin Laden had failed.
A low-cost incentive approach was proposed using the Taliban's desire for international contacts, without major rewards.
The Taliban's brush-off of the indictment may signal a shift from tolerance to more active support for Bin Laden.
